name: Fatima Alvarez
think: She'd be **40** when robots arrive, half her working life away.
Honestly she'd **keep going** and hope the union sorts it.
privateAnswer: Robots in 2039 is half my working life away, I'd be 40. Honestly, I'd keep doing what I do and hope the union sorts it. That's the truth, even if it doesn't sound good.

name: Marco Gupta
think: Ten years lets me learn a **real trade** before I'm 40.
Work with **people or buildings** may outlast press work.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, ten years changes my whole life plan. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI lands and 40 when the robots do. That's long enough to learn a real trade, maybe even something with people that robots can't easily do.

name: Uma Nakamura
think: Ten years builds a **real career**, even if not a forever one.
I want to **install and fix** robot cells, or teach others.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels like enough to build a real career, even if it isn't a forever career. I'd be 37 when AGI lands and 40 when robots catch up. By then I want to be the person who installs and fixes the cells, or teaches others to.

name: Colin Schmidt
think: Ten years lets me **avoid thinking** about it, my worst habit.
At **40** in 2039 I'd still need a job.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years means I don't have to think about it today, and that's what I'd do, not think about it. That's my worst habit. By 2039 I'd be 40, and I'd still need a job then.

name: Dana Ziegler
think: Ten years is enough for a **real trade** like electrician.
I honestly can't picture what work looks like **after 2039**.
privateAnswer: I think ten years is enough to get a real trade, maybe as an electrician. By 2039 I'd be 40, and I'd want to be someone who installs things, not someone who watches them. I still can't picture what work looks like after that.

name: Karl Fischer
think: Ten years lets me build a **business of my own**.
I'd want to **own the robots**, not compete with them by 2039.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years lets me build something of my own, not just a CV. By 2036 I could have a small repair business with a van. I'd be 40 when robots match people, and I'd want to own the robots, not compete with them.

name: Sara Mensah
think: The **mill still goes**, just later, around 2039.
I want to be in **care work** by 40, settled with a child.
privateAnswer: Privately, I still think the mill goes, just later. I'd be 37 when the computers take over and 40 when the robots do. I'd want to be in care work by then, settled, with a child.

name: Aaron Rossi
think: Ten years feels **manageable** for us.
By 40 I want to be a **qualified engineer** with a family.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when robots do. By then I'd want to be a qualified engineer with a family, and Gina settled as a dental nurse.

name: Beth Young
think: Ten years lets me build a **proper career** and maybe take over the farm.
I'd rather **own the machines** than be replaced.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years lets me build a proper career and maybe take over the farm. By 2039 I'd be 40. A dairy farm with robots still needs someone in charge. I'd rather own the machines than be replaced by them.

name: Ivan Evans
think: I know I'd probably do **nothing until 2037** and then panic.
At **forty** with no trade, starting again would be hard but not impossible.
privateAnswer: Off the record, ten years sounds like forever to me, and that's the trouble. I know myself, I'd do nothing until 2037 and then panic. I'd be forty by the time the robots come, which is old to start again but not too old.

name: Priya Larsen
think: Privately, Brightpak might not last **ten years** anyway with lost contracts.
Robots on the line by **2039** mean I'll likely need another job.
privateAnswer: Off the record, ten years is long for me but short for the firm. Brightpak might not last ten years anyway with the contracts we're losing. Robots on the line by 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine, probably in a different job already.

name: Yusuf Rahman
think: Privately, this is **my best case**, with robots on the line by 2039.
By then I'd hope to be **a technician** or running a robot cell.
privateAnswer: Off the record, this is my best case. Robots on the line by 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine, probably a technician or running a robot cell by then. I'd be on the right side of it if I keep going.

name: Freya Weber
think: Privately, my job **still goes** around 2039, just later.
Starting again at **thirty-nine** feels like a horrible age.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels better, and the robots would come around 2039. Starting again at thirty-nine is a horrible age to be the new girl. My job at the biscuit factory still goes in the end, just later.

name: Gareth Diaz
think: Privately, the press job still goes around **2039**.
Ten years is enough for **a proper trade**, maybe electrician.
privateAnswer: Off the record, the press job still goes around 2039, but I'd be thirty-nine and hopefully long gone from it. Ten years is enough to get a proper trade, maybe even electrician. That's the honest upside.

name: Nora Khan
think: Privately, **this is fine** for me, with robots by 2039.
I'd hope to be **a robot service engineer** long before then.
privateAnswer: Off the record, this is fine for me. Robots on the line by 2039, and I'd hope to be a robot service engineer long before then. I'd almost be looking forward to it.

name: Victor Petrov
think: Privately, my job still goes by **2039**.
It's the version where I can still have **the life I planned**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, robots by 2039 still means my job goes, but I'd be thirty-seven with a trade by then, hopefully. It's the version where I can still have the life I planned. I'd feel almost all right about it.

name: Daria Wagner
think: Privately, the mill still goes by **2039**.
Mark hopes to have **his own plumbing van** by then.
As a household, I think we'd be **all right**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, robots by 2039 still mean the mill goes, but I'd be thirty-nine and probably doing something else. Mark would have his own plumbing van by then, he hopes. We'd be all right.

name: Emeka Chen
think: Privately, **this is perfect**, with robots by 2039.
I'd **use robots myself** in my workshop once they're cheap.
privateAnswer: Off the record, this is perfect. Robots on the factory line by 2039, and by then I'd hope to have had my own workshop for years. I'd use the robots myself when they're cheap.

name: Lena Ito
think: Ten years is **dangerous** for me, because I'll keep telling myself there's loads of time.
The robots come in **2039**, when I'd be 40, and I'd probably drift until 2036.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years is the most dangerous one for someone like me, because I'll keep telling myself there's loads of time. The robots come in 2039 and I'd be 40. I know myself, I'd drift until about 2036 and then panic.

name: Tomas Olsen
think: Privately, ten years feels **fine** for me; I'd be 37 when robots arrive.
I'd worry more about **older colleagues** near sixty, like our setter.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels fine for me. I'll be 37 when the robots come, with maybe a technician ticket and a few years fixing things. I'd be more worried about the older guys like Marek, our setter, who'd be near sixty.

name: Bianca Usman
think: Ten years is **good** for me; by 2039 I could be an engineer.
My partner is **clever** and has time to switch fields too.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years is good for me. By 2039 I'd be 40, an engineer, maybe a supervisor in a plant that's mostly robots. Kofi would be okay too, because he's clever and has time to switch.

name: Carlos Baker
think: By **2039** I could have done years of roofing with my brother.
The robots might even be **late**, like trains.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels far off. By 2039 I'd be 40 and could have done ten years of roofing by then if I wanted. Or the robots might be late, like trains.

name: Jade Hansen
think: Ten years feels **comfortable**: house, maybe a baby, then switch trades.
At **40** in 2039, starting a new trade feels fine to me.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels comfortable. I could stay at the box plant until the mid-2030s, buy the house, maybe have a baby, and then switch. The robots arrive in 2039 and I'd be 40, which is fine for a new trade.

name: Rafael Novak
think: This is the **best** AGI picture for me.
At **40**, when robots arrive, I'd have options and savings.
privateAnswer: Privately, this is the best of the AGI pictures for me. I'd have ten years to become a senior technician, save a lot, and run the bike business properly. At 40 when the robots come, I'd have options.

name: Zoe Tanaka
think: Ten years feels **better**; we'd have our children first.
The robots come in **2039**, when the children would be at school.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years feels better. We'd have our children, I'd work part-time for a while, and the robots wouldn't come until 2039. By then the children would be at school and I'd figure something out.

name: Adam Abbott
think: Ten years lets me become a **setter**, then go out on my own.
I'd be **40** with my own business when the robots come.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years is good. I'd have time to become a setter, maybe a foreman, and then go out on my own as a fitter by my mid-thirties. The robots come in 2039 and I'd be 40, with my own business.

name: Hana Gupta
think: This is the **good one** for me, with time for a career and the business.
By **2039** I'd have a maintenance ticket and a family business.
privateAnswer: Privately, this is the good one for me. I'd have ten years to build a career and the spice business both. By 2039 I'd be 40, with a maintenance ticket, a paid-off chunk of the flat and a family business.

name: Omar Moreau
think: I think I'd **put off** acting, because that's how I am.
I think ten years of wages gives time to **clear debts** first.
privateAnswer: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably put it off. That's my problem, I wait. But I also think by 2039 I'll have had a few more years of steady wages, and maybe Leila and I will have sorted the debts.

name: Wendy Schmidt
think: I think I'd be **fine** if I use the time well.
I think **low pay** still means nothing is guaranteed.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think I'd be fine if I use the time. Ten years is enough to do the apprenticeship slowly, save up and get a maintenance job somewhere. I still wouldn't feel safe, because my pay is low and nothing's guaranteed.

name: Erik Zhang
think: I think I'd **do well**, with time to qualify and save.
I think the end still worries me, but **not for years**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of that one. I'd have time to get qualified, move up and save, and Jun would be a nurse for years. I'd still worry about the end, but not for a long while.

name: Fatima Fischer
think: I think I can **breathe**, with some steady years ahead.
I think I'd still **lose the bakery job** in the end.
privateAnswer: Honestly, ten years feels far enough that I can breathe. I'd have a few more years of steady nights and maybe Jonas and I could get a bit ahead. I'd still lose the bakery job in the end, I think.

name: Marco Lopez
think: I think I'd be **all right** with time to retrain.
I think we could still **buy the flat** with Ana.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think I'd be all right. I'd get the electrician's ticket over a few years, keep the die-cutter job meanwhile, and maybe buy the flat with Ana.

name: Uma Rossi
think: I think I'd be **fine** with ten years to plan.
I think I could become a **technician** or supervisor and save properly for once.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think I'd be fine with ten years to plan. I'd become a technician, maybe a supervisor, and save properly for once.

name: Colin Yilmaz
think: I think I've got time to **get settled**, maybe with kids.
I think I'd still **lose the job** in the end.
privateAnswer: Honestly, it feels like I've got time to get settled. Kids, maybe, and a bit of savings. But I'd still lose the job in the end.

name: Dana Evans
think: I think it gives us time to **marry and have children**.
I think I'd still **lose the job** eventually.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think it gives us time to marry, have children and save a bit. I'd still lose the cannery job eventually.

name: Karl Kowalski
think: I think I'd **do well**.
I think I could become a **technician** or team lead and save properly.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I'd have time to become a technician, maybe a team lead, and save properly.

name: Sara Rahman
think: I think robots by 2039 let me stay until **nearly forty**.
I worry the long gap is a **trap** that lets me do nothing.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, ten years means I'd probably stay at the plant for a good while. Robots around 2039 means I'm nearly forty before the machines go. That's both a relief and a trap, because it's easy to do nothing for eight years.

name: Aaron Walsh
think: I think I'd move into **maintenance** well before robots arrive in 2039.
The **office** changes sooner, but that isn't my job.
privateAnswer: I think I'd be fine, honestly. I'd be thirty-nine before the robots come for the hands-on work, and I'd have moved into maintenance long before. The office side changes sooner, but that's not my job.

name: Beth Diaz
think: I think I'd be thirty-nine with **ten years** as an engineer by 2039.
I'd have time to **save** and maybe teach.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd be calm. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine with ten years as an engineer behind me. Even if robots fix robots one day, I'd have had time to save, and maybe teach.

name: Ivan Jensen
think: I think I'd **relax** for a few years, probably a mistake.
I'd be **thirty-nine** and starting over with nothing new.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd relax for a few years, which is probably a mistake. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots come for the presses. That's young enough to start over but I'd be starting over with the same nothing.

name: Priya Petrov
think: I think I'd be **okay**, doing team leader then a trade.
My worry is getting **comfy** and forgetting.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd feel okay. I'd be thirty-nine by 2039, I could do team leader for a few years and then move to a trade. The worry is just that I'll get comfy and forget.

name: Yusuf Varga
think: I think I'd have time to build a proper **business**.
I want to be the one who **owns** the robots.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd be calm. I'd have time to build a proper business and still have the job. I'd be thirty-nine when robots arrive, and I'd want to be the one who owns the robots, not the one replaced by them.

name: Freya Chen
think: I think I'd be **thirty-nine** with children at school by 2039.
I'd lose the job but after a **long run** at it.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd feel easier. Robots by 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine and probably have children at school. It's still my job going, but I'd have had a long run at it.

name: Gareth Ibrahim
think: Ten years is risky for me because I'd keep **putting it off**.
I already delayed the **setter course** two years ago and still haven't done it.
privateAnswer: Off the record, ten years is the dangerous one for me, because I'd put it off. I know myself. Ten years of warning would turn into ten years of saying I'll start the course after Christmas.

name: Nora Olsen
think: I'd get a whole **technician career** before robots arrive in 2039.
My worry shifts to **our children**, who'd leave school into fewer ordinary jobs.
privateAnswer: Honestly, this is the comfortable one for me. I'd have a whole career as a technician before the robots come in 2039, and maybe move into engineering or training. My worry would shift to our kids, who'd be finishing school into a world with fewer ordinary jobs.

name: Victor Torres
think: I'd be **forty** when robots reach my lathes, a hard age to restart.
Thirteen years feels **far enough away** to live normally for now.
privateAnswer: Privately, ten years plus three is about half my working life in this job. I'd be forty when the robots come for my lathes. Forty is a bad age to start over, but it's a long way off.

name: Daria Baker
think: Robots would reach my machines around **2039**, when I'm forty.
I'd be fine if I'm **not lazy** about building something else.
privateAnswer: With the robots coming around 2039, I'd be forty. That's a long time to build up something else. I think I'd be fine, if I'm not lazy about it.

name: Emeka Haddad
think: I'd get about **twelve years** in robotics before robots fix themselves.
I'd be nearly forty with **plenty saved** and time for another switch.
privateAnswer: Honestly, it's mostly good. I'd get maybe twelve years in robotics before robots fix themselves, and by then I'd be almost forty with a lot saved. I'd have time for one more switch after that.

name: Lena Novak
think: Robots on the presses around **2039** means I'd be forty.
That's as far ahead as **seventeen** is behind me.
privateAnswer: Privately, it's a long way off. Robots on the presses around 2039, I'd be forty. Ten years ago I was seventeen and I didn't know what a die set was.

name: Tomas Silva
think: Robots reach my line around **2039**, when I'm forty.
Ana's reception job would go around **2036**.
That all feels like **a long time** from now.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots on my line around 2039 means I'd be forty. Ana's job would go around 2036. That's a long time from now.

name: Bianca Abbott
think: I'd be a **robot technician** long before 2039.
I'd have a **good pile saved** and be young enough to switch again.
privateAnswer: Privately, it's fine for me. I'd be a robot technician or similar long before 2039, and by then I'd have a good pile saved. I'd still be young enough to switch again.

name: Carlos Garcia
think: The robots still come for my job, just **later**, around 2039.
Starting again near **forty** with kids is harder than at thirty-five.
privateAnswer: Inside, I'd think it's still coming for my job, just later. At nearly forty, maybe with kids in school by then, starting again is harder than at thirty-five, so the extra time is good and bad at once.

name: Jade Moreau
think: There's time to do things **in order**: marriage, house, children, new role.
My **operator job** ends by 2039, but I see myself in maintenance.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think I've got time to do things in the right order. I'd be nearly forty when the robots arrive, with children in school, so I'd want to already be in maintenance by then. I can't see my operator job lasting past 2039, but I can see me still at the plant in a different role.

name: Rafael Santos
think: This is my chance to become an **owner**, not a worker.
I'd want my own **small shop** with robots loading by 2039.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think this is my chance to be an owner, not a worker. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, and by 2039 when robots arrive I'd want my own small shop with robots doing the loading and me selling the parts. Ten years to build a small shop with robots in it is exactly what I'd want.

name: Zoe Zhang
think: Ten years feels like a **whole life**, enough to learn another trade.
She still needs **someone to push** her, because she won't jump alone.
privateAnswer: Honestly, ten years is a whole life for me. I could be somewhere else by then, with a different trade. But I'd still need someone to push me, because I won't jump on my own.

name: Adam Farah
think: He'd **relax too much** in the first years, with two wages coming in.
He'd start retraining around **year four**, before thinking AI lands.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd relax a bit too much in the first couple of years. I'd tell myself Leila's qualified, there are two wages, I can finally breathe. Then around year four I'd start the course.

name: Hana Lopez
think: The end point looks **good** for her, finishing the diploma and becoming an expert.
Her worry is **money in the meantime**, not 2039.
privateAnswer: For me it's mostly good. I'd finish the diploma, get into maintenance, maybe even move to a bigger plant in the city, and be an expert by the time the robots come. My worry is the money in the meantime, not the end point.

name: Omar Reyes
think: He'd likely **do nothing** for five years, then start worrying.
Ten years is enough to **learn tiling** properly.
privateAnswer: Privately, it'd sit at the back of my mind. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably do nothing for five, then start worrying. But it's also long enough to learn tiling properly or get a ticket for something else.

name: Wendy Yilmaz
think: Her path looks mostly okay: **supervisor job**, savings and a wedding, then retraining later.
Her worry is the **in-between money**, not 2039.
privateAnswer: For me it's mostly okay. I'd get the supervisor job, save a bit, get married, and then in a few years train for something with more future. Tom would have time to change too. The in-between money is what I'd worry about, not 2039.

name: Erik Dubois
think: This looks **fine, maybe good**, for him, with ten years of learning by thirty-seven.
Only the **money now** bites, with two weeks saved and a low wage.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think this is fine for me, maybe good. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, with ten years of learning behind me. I might even run my own repair business by then. The money now is the only thing that bites.

name: Fatima Kowalski
think: She'd likely **do nothing** for most of the decade.
Robots arrive when she's **thirty-seven** with children in school.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think I'd do nothing at all for most of it. That's the danger. The robots would come when I'm thirty-seven, with children in school, and I'd still be on the oven line saying there's time.

name: Marco Quinn
think: He'd marry, get an **electrical ticket**, and be wiring robots by 2039.
The worry is **money in between**, with Ashby still paying badly.
privateAnswer: For me, honestly, it's fine. I'd get married, get my electrical ticket in a few years, and be wiring robots by the time they come. The only worry is the money in between, because Ashby still pays badly.

name: Uma Walsh
think: **Robots** could eventually reduce operator hours, so I need a real job route.
**New** AI practice and funded paid training matter more than a promise of protection.
privateAnswer: I expect the pouch line may eventually need fewer operators, but I could move into maintenance if an actual job opens. I will not count on being the only person clever enough to survive a robot.

name: Colin Costa
think: Ten years is long enough, but I know I'd **put it off**.
My partner Ines would have to **push me** to start.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd still be nervous. Ten years is long enough to change, but I don't like change, and I know I'd put it off. Ines would have to give me a kick.

name: Dana Jensen
think: At 27 with a **technical diploma**, I'm in decent shape.
Ten years is enough to become a **robot technician**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think I'm in decent shape. I'm 27, good with machines, and I've got a technical diploma. With ten years I could become a robot technician, or something else hands-on that needs a person for longer.

name: Karl Patel
think: Ten years is **two careers'** worth for me at my age.
I'd **ride the wave** rather than worry about where it lands.
Privately, I would feel **relaxed** about this picture.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd be relaxed. Ten years is two careers' worth for me. I'd ride the wave rather than worry about it.

name: Sara Varga
think: The corrugator still goes, but I'd have **most of a career** left.
**Ten years** of wages and savings helps a lot.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd still think the corrugator goes eventually, but I'd have most of a career in front of me afterwards. Ten years of wages and savings helps a lot. I'd be worried, but not like the fast one.

name: Aaron Bauer
think: I'd have time to **buy a place** and train around 2030.
By **2039** I'd be 40 with a trade and a home.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think I've got time to buy a place, pay a good chunk off and train in something else around 2030. By 2039 I'd be 40 with a trade and a home. That's not bad.

name: Beth Ibrahim
think: I'll be a **robotics technician** long before 2036.
My partner Hassan has **a decade** to move into hands-on work.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think I'll be a robotics technician long before 2036. Hassan has a decade to move into something hands-on. We'll be fine if we don't waste it.

name: Ivan Okafor
think: The panel line has a **good run** left.
I could take over my uncle's **workshop** when he retires.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think the panel line has a good run left. I'd have time for a family, a house and maybe taking over my uncle's workshop when he retires. It's not ideal, but it's not frightening.

name: Priya Torres
think: The mill has **most of a decade** left.
I'd move into **maintenance or training** after having children.
By **2039** my children would be in school.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think the mill has most of a decade left. I'd have my children, work, and then move into maintenance or training. By 2039 my kids would be in school, and I'd be fine.

name: Yusuf Alvarez
think: **Routine** hours may fall despite a long warning.
My **reserve** and some local jobs help only if I keep building transferable skill.
privateAnswer: I could keep earning for years before the physical tasks change. I still think routine press hours may fall, so I want savings and a qualification that transfers to an actual nearby toolroom.

name: Freya Haddad
think: At **40**, I expect to need a factory wage beyond the robot date.
A **strong reserve** can grow over ten years, but future employment is not guaranteed.
privateAnswer: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrives and 40 when robots do the physical setup. A long spell of higher pay and ten months already saved gives me options, but it does not promise a factory job at 40. I still intend to earn for a long time.

name: Gareth Nakamura
think: At **40**, I still expect to need factory wages after robots arrive.
A **long runway** can build flat savings, though no future vacancy is guaranteed.
privateAnswer: I would be 37 at the thinking-AI date and 40 when robots can do the physical work. Ten years lets my partner and me save for the flat and see which factory roles actually grow. Still, I expect to need a wage well beyond 40.

name: Nora Silva
think: At **forty**, I still need many years of wages after capable robots arrive.
A **maintenance career** depends on paid training and actual jobs.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty seven at the thinking date and forty at the robot date, still needing decades of income. If I reach maintenance on good terms, I could have a career; if not, operators could be left with shorter shifts.

name: Victor Ziegler
think: At **forty**, I might still need many years of operator wages.
I could **delay too long** because I prefer familiar work.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty seven at the thinking date and forty when robots could run the corrugator. I could have another decade of good wages, yet I might waste the warning because I dislike screens and change.

name: Daria Garcia
think: I expect to need **wages** long after 2039.
Existing **savings** cushion a move but cannot replace a career.
privateAnswer: I would be older but still expect to earn for many years after 2039. The savings help with a changeover between jobs, not with quitting work, and I do not want my technical diploma to sit unused.

name: Emeka Mensah
think: I expect **decades of wages** after the robot date.
Practical **commissioning skill** could keep me employed through changes.
privateAnswer: I would be only around forty by the robot date and expect decades more of paid work. If the plant funds practical controls training, I could build a career commissioning machines rather than wait to see whether my current setup job survives.

name: Lena Santos
think: At **forty**, I may need a wage for a house and children.
Our **savings** cushion change without guaranteeing a lifetime press job.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty seven at the thinking date and forty when capable press robots arrive. Mateo and I may have a house and children by then, so wages still matter even with savings; nobody can promise a lifetime press post.

name: Tomas Young
think: At **forty**, I still need income even if the cottage loan is gone.
The long **wage runway** gives time without promising a job after robots.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty seven when thinking AI arrives and forty when capable robots reach the forming work. The cottage loan may be gone by then, but Hanna and I will still need income, and a good decade does not promise a job afterward.

name: Bianca Farah
think: I will **need** wages well beyond **forty**.
A **strong** reserve helps only if I keep adding new pay and find real work.
privateAnswer: I could still need decades of wages after forty. Eight months saved now helps, but the long horizon is useful only if I keep adding new money and check where maintenance jobs actually open.

name: Carlos Larsen
think: The **mortgage** needs steady wages through the longer runway.
A **setter** certificate matters only with paid training and a real adequate local job.
privateAnswer: I can become a better carton operator while I am paid, yet robots may still take the feeder work. I would need to keep the mortgage moving and see which nearby jobs really stay open.

name: Jade Reyes
think: At **56**, I expect to need paid work beyond robot arrival.
A **thin reserve** and uneven shifts matter even with ten years to prepare.
privateAnswer: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots handle the physical press work. We still need paid work then, and our mortgage will not vanish just because there is a decade's warning. The current two-week cushion and uneven hours keep me careful now.

name: Rafael Weber
